findings.where: Article specimen, from the TV-studio photograph's caption through the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?', the three-item list and the rule above the PDF link, at both widths
findings.fault: The rhythm comes apart exactly where the brief asked for proof that it holds. The caption sits right against the subhead below it, with no space between, so it reads as part of the subhead rather than as the photo's caption. The list is set solid: its lines are closer together than the paragraph above, so it looks like a different text pasted in. Its last item runs straight into the rule and the PDF link. Each new kind of content (image, caption, subhead, list) changes the spacing, which is the opposite of one rhythm that holds when content is added.
findings.who_objects: The founder and round 1's critics, who made 'the look must survive Angélique's content' a condition of this round and asked for this specimen to show it. Angélique would also object: every article she adds with a photo or a list would look broken.

findings.where: First screen, the blue field: the diagonal hatching across the whole field and the ghosted giant 'PPP' letters behind the first lines of the heading (on the phone, a cropped 'PP' behind the caption and heading)
findings.fault: The direction is 'one field of blue', and the tile's own Texture panel says 'No texture: one flat field, no grain and no gradient'. But the hero is covered in diagonal stripes and carries a second, ghosted display word behind Mark's line. The stripes make the field busy, and on screen they read as hatching or a technical drawing. The ghost 'PPP' adds an element where the research asks for scale contrast, not more elements. It also muddies 'In my view', the words that should land first.
findings.who_objects: Several people would object. The founder judges the first screen first and would be shown a tile that contradicts its own specimen. Mark finds busy sites off-putting and has said nothing should read as 'techy'. A development-bank reader would see a pattern and an acronym before they see the sentence.

findings.where: First screen at phone width: the portrait, heading and 'Write to me at' action
findings.fault: On a phone the studio portrait comes first, at full width, and fills most of the first screen. Mark's line only starts near the bottom of the screen, and the one action is about a screen and a half down. So the first thing a phone visitor sees is a passport-style photo and a menu, with no message and no action. The desktop order (his words first, then the photo beside them) is reversed.
findings.who_objects: Development-bank staff who arrive from a LinkedIn link on their phone. The brief asks for one message and one action on the first screen, and this visitor gets neither without scrolling.

findings.where: Article specimen: the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?' against the article title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law', most of all at phone width
findings.fault: The subhead is set as large as the article's title, and on the phone it looks larger. Squinting at the article, a section heading competes with the title, so the reader cannot tell at a glance which is the page's title and which is a part of it.
findings.who_objects: A reader of Mark's articles, who uses the size steps to see the article's structure. Angélique would also object: her subheads would look like new articles.

findings.where: First screen, the area next to the one action (the lead paragraph, the labels row and 'Write to me at')
findings.fault: The first screen says what Mark does and for whom. It gives nothing a visitor could check: no region or place of his work, no named body that asked for it, and no recent talk or article. The topic labels are claims, not evidence. A visitor deciding whether to write has only the portrait and a sentence to go on.
findings.who_objects: Development-bank and agency staff, who select advisers against terms of reference by region and kind of work. They want to see that he has done this work, and where, before they write.
